newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Turkish Cypriots unfazed by missile row.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Cypriots unfazed by missile row.

text.p: Turkish Cypriots say they are not troubled by a Greek Cypriot move to buy Russian anti- aircraft missiles but fear the well-publicised row will further damage tourism on the divided island.
"We are not panicked at all -- thanks to the motherland (Turkey). We know it will protect us," Sefer Inaloz, a retired hospital worker, said. "There is more alarm in Turkey."
The Cypriot government announced an agreement with Moscow this month to buy Russian S-300 missiles which it says are needed against any threat of an air raid from Turkey.
Turkey says the missiles are offensive weapons because they can also hit planes in Turkish airspace. It has threatened a military strike to stop their deployment.
Bellicose statements from top Turkish officials were criticised in the West, but Turkish Cypriots welcomed them as proof of mainland Turks' backing for their ethnic kin on Cyprus.
"We don't want any fighting...But it is such statements that give us peace of mind," said Sule Kelesoglu, a chemist in the northern resort town of Kyrenia.

Turkish Cypriots in Kyrenia and the north of the divided capital Nicosia said they did not believe the Greek Cypriots had any plan to use the missiles -- which are not due to be delivered for at least 16 months.
Many pointed to Turkish military superiority and dismissed the missile threat as mere political manoeuvring.

"I am not worried about the missiles at all, because this is just another piece of Greek Cypriot propaganda for the world, for it to try and put itself in the right in their eyes," said civil servant Ayhan Akkurt.
"They have proved before that their propaganda trips are nothing -- they don't have the guts. That is what happened with the bikers' action, which was a complete fiasco," Akkurt added.

Last year, Greek Cypriot motorcyclists organised a protest against the division of the island which was to involve driving over the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone. The rally was cancelled but some bikers went ahead and two Greek Cypriots were killed in the subsequent troubles.
Many Turkish Cypriots were more worried about the bad press the missile row was giving the island than the prospect of war.

"I'm most worried about tourism," said jeweller Omer Kansu, 32. "With all this disputing, this year will be a washout again. It is always happening, after the biker incident tourists cancelled their holidays here. They are playing with our bread."

Northern Cyprus, which declared itself a state in 1983 but is recognised only by Turkey, relies heavily on tourism. Its economy is labouring under Western sanctions and its per capita gross domestic product (GDP) is much lower than the south's.

Cyprus has been divided since Turkish troops invaded in 1974 in response to a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Hostility between the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities dates back to the early 1960s.
Turkish Cypriots say after decades of tension, they cannot see how the missile purchase can make the situation any worse.

"I think the whole thing is hot air," said Akile Nacisoy, 18, who works in a shoe shop. "Why would they use such weapons in such a small place? If they did, the Greek Cypriots would die as well as the Turks -- they would blow the whole place up."
Some were confident that the West would not allow conflict.
"There won't be war. The big countries -- the United States, Britain and France -- won't allow that and everything will end peacefully, I am sure," said hospital worker Inaloz.

A U.S. envoy sent to the island over the row said on Monday the crisis had been defused because the Cypriot government of President Glafcos Clerides had assured him it would not import the missiles for at least 16 months.
